messages.subject: Working with sparse count data - IPM including immigration
messages.subject_clean: Working with sparse count data - IPM including immigration
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

I am hoping to get some advice about running an IPM with sparse count data. The estimates obtained from my IPM model are higher than those obtained from the single dataset analyses, suggesting that there is a demographic process adding individuals into the system that I am not accounting for. Additionally, when running posterior predictive checks my Bayesian p-values suggest that the model is underfitting the data. As such, I am trying to include immigration in the model, but my count data are very sparse (total of 6 observed counts over my 25-year time series) therefore making immigration nonidentifiable. Including immigration in the model does improve the fit, but I am unable to get the immigration component to converge.

I’m working on giving some more informative priors (but have very limited information about immigration in the species to go on) but was wondering if anyone has experience working with very sparse count data. I've tried a model assuming a constant number of individuals immigrating across time, but that model fit the data poorly. I am trying to make sure that I move forward with a model that fits the data well and provides unbiased parameter estimates but am finding it difficult to obtain convergence given the lack of information in my count data. Any advice or suggestions would be greatly appreciated! Below is a copy of my model code with estimation of absolute number of immigrants included.

# model code

# Adapted from examples in Kéry and Schaub (2012) and Schaub and Kéry (2021).

cat(file="ZIGP_immigration.txt", "
model {
# Priors and constraints
for (i in 1:nind){
   for (t in f[i]:(n.occasions-1)){
      phi[i,t]<- alpha[age[i,t],t]  # Constrain survival to be age-specific
      } #t
   } #i

# Priors for age and time specific survival
for (u in 1:2){
for (t in 1:(n.occasions-1)){
   alpha[u,t] ~ dunif(0, 1)
   }
}

# Prior for time specific fecundity
for (t in 1:(n.occasions-1)){
  fecund [t] ~ dunif(0, 1)
}

# Constrain expected number of immigrants to mean plus time-specific error
  for (t in 1:n.occasions){
    log(omega[t]) <- log.b0.om <http://log.b0.om> + err.om <http://err.om>[t]
    err.om <http://err.om>[t] ~ dnorm(0, tau.om <http://tau.om>)
  }

# Priors for immigration variance parameters
  tau.om <http://tau.om> <- pow(sigma.om <http://sigma.om>, -2)
  sigma.om <http://sigma.om> ~ dunif(0, 10)
  sigma2.om <http://sigma2.om> <- pow(sigma.om <http://sigma.om>, 2)

# Prior for mean expected number of immigrants
  b0.om <http://b0.om> ~ dunif(0, 250)

# Back-transformation of mean expected number of immigrants
  log.b0.om <http://log.b0.om> <- log(b0.om <http://b0.om>)

# Prior for mean expected # encounters per individual
  epsilon ~ dgamma(1,1)

# Prior for probability of availablity at time t given absense at time t-1
  gamma[1] ~ dbeta(1, 1)

# Prior for probability of availablity at time t given available at time t-1
  gamma[2] ~ dbeta(1, 1)

# Prior for overdispersion parameter (defines individual heterogeneity in detection)
  theta ~ dunif(0,250)

###############################################################
################### Population model ###############################
###############################################################

# Population count data (state-space model)
# Model for the initial stage-specific population sizes: uniform priors

N1  ~ dnorm(100,0.01)I(0,)  # First year individuals
N[1,1] <- round(N1)
N2  ~ dnorm(100,0.01)I(0,)  # Second year individuals
N[2,1] <- round(N2)
N3  ~ dnorm(100,0.01)I(0,)  # Third year individuals
N[3,1] <- round(N3)
N4 ~ dnorm(200,0.01)I(0,)   # Fourth year individuals
N[4,1] <- round(N4)
N5 ~ dnorm(200,0.01)I(0,)   # Fifth year and older individuals
N[5,1] <- round(N5)
I[1] ~ dpois(omega[1])        # Immigrants

# Process model over time: our model of population dynamics
for (t in 1:(n.occasions-1)){
  N[1,t+1] ~ dbin((fecund[t] / 2) * alpha[1,t], Ntot[t])
  N[2,t+1] ~ dbin(alpha[1,t], N[1,t])
  N[3,t+1] ~ dbin(alpha[1,t], N[2,t])
  N[4,t+1] ~ dbin(alpha[1,t], N[3,t])
  N[5,t+1] ~ dbin(alpha[2,t], Ntot[t])
  I[t+1] ~ dpois(omega[t+1])
}

# Observation model
for (t in 1:n.occasions){
  Ntot[t] <- N[4,t] + N[5,t] + I[t]
  C[t] ~ dpois(Ntot[t])

# GoF for population count data: mean absolute percentage error
    C.pred[t] ~ dpois(Ntot[t])
    disc.C[t] <- pow(((C[t] - Ntot[t]) / C[t]) * ((C[t] - Ntot[t]) / (C[t] + 0.001)), 0.5)  # Add a small number to avoid potential division by 0
    discN.C[t] <- pow(((C.pred[t] - Ntot[t]) / (C.pred[t] + 0.001)) * ((C.pred[t] - Ntot[t]) / (C.pred[t] + 0.001)), 0.5)
  }
  fit.C <- 100 / n.occasions * sum(disc.C)
  fitN.C <- 100 / n.occasions * sum(discN.C)

###############################################################
####### Productivity model ##########################################
###############################################################

# Productivity data (Binomial regression model)
for (t in 1:(n.occasions-1)){
    J[t] ~ dbin(fecund[t], nbrood[t])    # number young observed as fledged
    Jrep[t] ~ dbin(fecund[t], nbrood[t]) # Replicate data for GOF
    }

# Compute posterior predictive checks statistics
for (t in 1:(n.occasions-1)){
    Jexp[t] <- fecund[t]* nbrood[t]
    Jchi[t] <- (J[t] - Jexp[t])^2 / (Jexp[t] + 0.5)
    Jchi.new[t] <- (Jrep[t] - Jexp[t])^2 / (J[t] + 0.5)
}

  fit.fecund <- sum(Jchi[1:(n.occasions-1)])
  fit.fecund.new <http://fit.fecund.new> <- sum(Jchi.new[1:(n.occasions-1)])

###############################################################
################ CJS model #######################################
###############################################################
# Zero-inflated gamma-Poisson adapted from Riecke et al. (2022)
# To account for heterogeniety in observation process and overdispersion

# CMR Model Likelihood components
for (i in 1:nind){

h[i] ~ dgamma(theta, theta)

   for (t in (f[i]+1):n.occasions){

      z[i,t] ~ dbern(phi[i,t-1] * z[i,t-1])

      # State process
      a[i,t] ~ dbern(mu1[i,t])
      mu1[i,t] <- z[i,t] * gamma[a[i,t-1]+1]

      # Observation process
      c[i,t] ~ dpois(mu2[i,t])
      mu2[i,t] <- a[i,t] * epsilon * h[i]
      } #t
   } #i

# Derived parameters
# Population growth rate
for (t in 1:(n.occasions-1)){
   lambda[t] <- Ntot[t+1] / Ntot[t]
   logla[t] <- log(lambda[t])
   }
mlam <- exp((1/(n.occasions-1))*sum(logla[1:(n.occasions-1)]))   # Geometric mean

} # end model
")

# Count data

count = c(NA,NA,NA,400,NA,543,NA,NA,NA,NA,NA,NA,NA,NA,NA,NA,NA,1425,NA,NA,2550,2190,NA,NA,2880)

The topic is broad and can be adapted to best fit the candidate's interests and skills.
